lines.text: HTML builds the page. Today CSS makes it beautiful, with colours, fonts and boxes.
HTML says what each part of the page is.
CSS says how it looks, like its colour, size and spacing.
We write CSS inside a style tag at the top of the page.
A rule starts with a selector, like h1, that picks what to style.
Inside curly brackets you write a property, a colon and a value.
Every property and value line ends with a semicolon.
The color property changes text colour, and background-color paints behind it.
You can use names like orange, or hex codes like ff9933 for saffron.
Pick colours that are easy to read together.
The font-family property picks the typeface, and font-size sets how big it is.
Always add a backup font, like sans-serif, in case the first one is missing.
Padding is the space inside a box, between the words and the border.
The border is the line around the box.
Margin is the space outside, pushing other boxes away.
The style tag holds our CSS, and this rule picks every h1 on the page.
The property is color, the value is orange, and a semicolon ends the line.
The body selector styles the whole page at once.
Arial is our first choice of font, and sans serif is the backup.
The border draws an orange line three pixels thick around the paragraph.
Padding pushes the words away from the border, and margin pushes other things away from the box.
Yellow on white looks bright, but it is very hard to read.
Dark text on a light background is clear for everyone, including people with weak eyesight.
The first rule is missing its colon, so the browser skips it.
The second rule still works, but a semicolon at the end is a good habit.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
